elements.id-string-9: Enjoyment of these videos is not simply a response to visual stimuli; rather, it hinges on the human capacity to understand (and appreciate) commonsense \emph{violations} depicted in these videos.We introduce \textbf{FunQA}, a challenging video question answering (QA) dataset specifically designed to evaluate and enhance the depth of video reasoning based on counter-intuitive and fun videos.
elements.id-string-10: Unlike most video QA benchmarks which focus on less surprising contexts, e.g., cooking or instructional videos, FunQA covers three previously unexplored types of surprising videos: \emph{1) HumorQA}, \emph{2) CreativeQA}, and \emph{3) MagicQA}.For each subset, we establish rigorous QA tasks designed to assess the model's capability in counter-intuitive timestamp localization, detailed video description, and reasoning around counter-intuitiveness.We also pose higher-level tasks, such as attributing a fitting and vivid title to the video, and scoring the video creativity.In total, the FunQA benchmark consists of 312K free-text QA pairs derived from 4.3K video clips, spanning a total of 24 video hours.Extensive experiments with existing VideoQA models reveal significant performance gaps for the FunQA videos across spatial-temporal reasoning, visual-centered reasoning, and free-text generation.

elements.id-string-27: To address this gap and evaluate computer vision models' ability to identify and understand visual commonsense violations in videos, we introduce \textbf{FunQA}, a comprehensive and high-quality VideoQA dataset comprising 4.3K surprising videos and 312K manually annotated free-text QA pairs.
elements.id-string-28: Our dataset consists of three subsets: \emph{1) HumorQA}, \emph{2) CreativeQA}, and \emph{3) MagicQA}.

elements.id-string-36: \textit{3) Counter-intuitiveness reasoning}: a model must generate concrete explanations of why the video is surprising.

elements.id-string-56: While the visual question answering (VQA) task focuses on enhancing models' ability in image comprehension \cite{goyal2017making, zhu2016visual7w, krishna2016visual}, video question answering (VideoQA) shifts the attention towards video comprehension.
elements.id-string-57: VideoQA is generally more challenging than VQA as it requires a comprehensive understanding of visual content, utilization of temporal and spatial information, and exploration of relationships between recognized objects and activities~\cite{yi2020clevrer}.
elements.id-string-58: To address the VideoQA task, the research community has introduced various benchmarks.
elements.id-string-59: As depicted in Table \ref{T:main}, Most commonly used VideoQA datasets are sourced from human-centric videos like movies \cite{tapaswi2016movieqa}, TV shows \cite{lei2018tvqa, lei2019tvqa, garcia2020knowit}, and social media \cite{jang-IJCV-2019, zadeh2019social, xiao2021nextqanext, grundemclaughlin2021agqa, yang2022avqa, wu2021star, castro2022fiber}, and there are also object-centric datasets of game videos \cite{mun2017marioqa}, synthetic videos \cite{yi2020clevrer} and egocentric videos~\cite{Gao_2021_ICCV}.
elements.id-string-60: MovieQA \cite{tapaswi2016movieqa} and TVQA \cite{lei2018tvqa} are commonly employed by VideoQA methods, which put forward tasks related to temporal and causal reasoning.
elements.id-string-61: However, they rely heavily on dialogue comprehension and textual plot summaries, which severely limits the challenge of visual reasoning.
elements.id-string-62: TGIF-QA \cite{jang-IJCV-2019} uses animated GIFs to challenge spatial-temporal reasoning, but as most GIFs are short videos of 3 seconds, and its tasks mainly focus on action description, TGIF-QA lacks complex reasoning evaluation ability.
elements.id-string-63: When most datasets use multiple choice questions as QA tasks, some methods, such as NExT-QA \cite{xiao2021nextqanext}, try to join open-ended questions.
elements.id-string-64: NExT-QA mainly focuses on daily life videos, but the open-ended answers are mostly simple sentences containing only a few words.
elements.id-string-65: To sum up, most existing methods focus on ordinary videos, lack of understanding of intriguing or unexpected videos, and advanced reasoning tasks such as generating complete explanatory texts of videos remain to be explored.
elements.id-string-67: Earlier studies have explored various models, including LSTMs and graph-based neural networks, to capture cross-modal information \cite{li2019beyond, zhao2018open}.
elements.id-string-68: With the advent of Transformers, video understanding models like ClipBERT \cite{leiless} and CoMVT \cite{seo2021look} emerged, focusing on the comprehension of specific frames within a video.

elements.id-string-72: Furthermore, recent Vision Language Models (VLMs) such as \cite{li2023otter,2023videochat,maaz2023videochatgpt} have showcased remarkable video understanding capabilities.

elements.id-string-85: In constructing the dataset, we adhered to three principles to address the challenges in video understanding capabilities: our dataset, FunQA, is \textbf{visual centered} and emphasizes \textbf{counter-intuitive reasoning}, \textbf{spatial-temporal reasoning}.
elements.id-string-86: Based on these principles, we collect 4365 videos from 3 different art genres and created three subsets: HumorQA, CreativeQA, and MagicQA.
elements.id-string-88: HumorQA composed of 1,769 meticulously curated web videos, serves as a unique source of insight into human humor comprehension.
elements.id-string-89: Notably, it contains the shortest average video length of 7s among the three subsets.
elements.id-string-90: We believe that the human process of understanding humor is complex and deep, requiring a holistic understanding of the video and adding a degree of common sense to it.
elements.id-string-91: Psychological research has demonstrated that humor arises from the incongruity \cite{kant1987critique,sep-humor} between reality and expectations, flourishing with the skillful juxtaposition and transformation of events \cite{latta1999basic,boyd2004laughter,koestler2020act}.
elements.id-string-92: This makes humorous videos a valuable asset for the VideoQA dataset, anticipated to enhance a model's proficiency in integrating information and performing deep reasoning.
elements.id-string-94: CreativeQA is a collection of 927 videos averaging 48s in length from a TV show called Kasou Taishou \cite{ntv}.
elements.id-string-95: This program, showcasing original and novel skits performed by various amateur groups and judged by a panel, boasts a strong creative flair
elements.id-string-97: The essence of the show lies in using a mix of people and props to mimic reality, with audiences deriving pleasure from information integration and comparison.
elements.id-string-98: We anticipate that the imitation nature of the show will challenge the model's capacity for information extraction, while the longer video length and need for understanding creativity will put to test the model's comprehension of spatial-temporal information.
elements.id-string-100: MagicQA encapsulates 1672 magic performance videos sourced from across the web, spanning various genres like camera magic, close-up magic, and stage magic.
elements.id-string-101: The essence of magic revolves around the creation of seemingly impossible illusions \cite{nelms2012magic}, employing diverse effects such as disappearance, creation, and transformation.
elements.id-string-102: These illusions are infused with abundant spatial-temporal information.
elements.id-string-103: Through this dataset, we aim to empower the model to not only track the ensuing changes in objects but also unravel the underlying mechanics \cite{lamont2005magic} of these transformations.
elements.id-string-105: To comprehensively evaluate the model's ability to understand surprising videos, we designed the following 4 types of tasks for each subset:
elements.id-string-107: The localization task is the base task to assess the model's comprehension abilities.
elements.id-string-108: It involves localizing counter-intuitive segments within the video, answers expressed in either seconds or frames.
elements.id-string-109: This task serves as the basis for the subsequent two main tasks in the three subsets, where the focus shifts to locating moments of humor, creativity, and magical effects, respectively.
elements.id-string-110: Successfully completing this task demands the model's understanding of the video's overall content, incorporating both temporal and spatial information.
elements.id-string-112: The description task aims to evaluate the model's information extraction capabilities, serving as a fundamental aspect of video understanding.
elements.id-string-113: Across all three subsets, this task requires providing a free-text answer that describes the selected moment.
elements.id-string-114: Furthermore, this task allows for analysis of how the model extracts information and generates answers for subsequent tasks.
elements.id-string-115: By examining the model's performance in this task, we gain insights into its ability to extract relevant information and generate meaningful responses.
elements.id-string-117: The reasoning task is designed to test the model's ability to reason about the video, and in the three subsets, this question is Why Humorous, Why creative, and Why counter-intuitive and the answer is a free-text explanation.
elements.id-string-118: This task is very difficult and involves the model's deep reasoning ability; it requires the model to give a complete explanation using information from the entire video and its own common sense.
elements.id-string-120: In addition to the three main tasks, we design higher-level tasks to enhance the model's inference abilities on counter-intuitive videos.
elements.id-string-121: \textit{Title Task} in HumorQA and CreativeQA requires generating a concise title summarizing the video's content.
elements.id-string-122: \textit{Creative Scoring Task} in CreativeQA involves rating the creativity of videos between 0 and 20.

elements.id-string-219: Overall, the performance of the models on the FunQA dataset is generally unsatisfactory, and we have made several key findings:
elements.id-string-220: \textbf{Timestamp localization task is the most challenging.}
elements.id-string-221: Caption-based models, due to their emphasis on captioning tasks, tend to provide descriptions of the entire video even when tasked with timestamp localization (refer to Appendix \ref{appendix_c: Failure of t1}).
elements.id-string-222: Conversely, instruction-based models, which are typically derived from image-based VLMs, focus on specific keyframes rather than considering the entire temporal space of the video.
elements.id-string-224: Caption-based models excel in providing detailed descriptions but struggle in tasks that require reasoning, resulting in a notable performance gap between description tasks (e.g., H2) and reasoning tasks (e.g., H3).
elements.id-string-225: On the other hand, instruction-based models demonstrate stronger reasoning capabilities but tend to underperform in description tasks.
elements.id-string-226: One possible explanation is that instruction-based models may generate excessive information in their answers, including a significant amount of incorrect information.
elements.id-string-227: \textbf{Performance varies greatly across different video types.}
elements.id-string-228: Most models can get a relatively accurate answer in humor and magic videos but have difficulty answering the questions in creative videos.
elements.id-string-229: One possible reason is that humor and magic videos often depict daily life that models have encountered previously, whereas creative videos contain content that models have never seen before, rendering them unable to generate new ideas and resulting in irrelevant and erroneous answers.
elements.id-string-231: Traditional metrics yield near-zero scores on free-text questions, as they solely focus on short textual similarity.
elements.id-string-232: While BLEURT scores are significantly higher, they still fall short in evaluating more complex similarities.
elements.id-string-233: Intuitively, GPT-4 is found to show preliminary capabilities in assessing free-text in deep understanding, which will be detailed in Appendix \ref{appendix_c: Evaluation Metrics}.
elements.id-string-234: However, there are still issues of instability, where the same content can receive different scores.
elements.id-string-235: \textbf{Finetuned Otter performs well on traditional metrics but lags behind in GPT-4 score.}
elements.id-string-236: We finetuned Otter on Dense Caption and FunQA, and Otter (FunQA) shows obvious performance advantages over Otter (D.C.).
elements.id-string-237: While Otter performs better in traditional metrics like ROUGE-L compared with other instruction-based models, the GPT-4 score of Otter (FunQA) underperforms.
elements.id-string-238: One possible reason revealed is that the input of Otter is only 128 frames sampled from the video, which is insufficient for comprehensive reasoning.
elements.id-string-239: Besides, the discrepancy between Otter's scores on traditional metrics and GPT-4 matches our finding of the lack of evaluation metrics.

elements.id-string-330: The principle of the traditional metrics is relatively simple.
elements.id-string-331: The traditional metric principles are as follows.
elements.id-string-332: \textbf{BLEU-4} BLEU, full name is Bilingual Evaluation Understudy, is a commonly used machine translation evaluation metric.
elements.id-string-333: It evaluates how good a machine translation result is by comparing how well it matches the N-gram of one or more human-translated reference results, which is a sequence of N consecutive words.
elements.id-string-334: BLEU-4, i.e., evaluates how well a combination of two words (i.e., a binary) matches.
elements.id-string-335: BLEU introduces a correction factor, Brevity Penalty (BP), to avoid this problem, which penalizes machine translation if the result is shorter than the reference translation.
elements.id-string-336: The BLEU score is the geometric mean of the individual N-gram accuracy multiplied by the shortness penalty.
elements.id-string-337: That is, the score of BLEU takes into account the precision and length of the translation result.
elements.id-string-339: ROUGE, known as Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation, is a commonly used evaluation method for tasks such as automatic digesting and machine translation.
elements.id-string-340: ROUGE is mainly evaluated by comparing the overlap between the generated abstracts and the reference abstracts.
elements.id-string-341: Among them, ROUGE-L is an important variant of ROUGE, where L stands for Longest Common Subsequence (LCS), i.e., the longest common subsequence.
elements.id-string-342: Unlike the n-gram, the longest common subsequence does not require consecutive occurrences of items in the sequence.
elements.id-string-344: CIDEr, known as Consensus-based Image Description Evaluation, is an evaluation metric specifically designed for evaluating image description (Image Captioning) tasks.
elements.id-string-345: The main advantage of CIDEr is that it can capture more detailed information because it uses TF-IDF weights to emphasize n-grams that occur frequently in manual annotation but are not common in all image descriptions.
elements.id-string-347: BLEURT, full name Bilingual Evaluation Understudy with Representations from Transformers, is an evaluation method based on the transformer model, specifically for evaluating the output quality of machine translation and natural language generation tasks.
elements.id-string-348: Unlike traditional evaluation metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE, BLEURT does not directly compare the n-gram match between generated text and reference text but uses pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) to understand the semantic information of text.
elements.id-string-349: the advantage of BLEURT is that it can capture the deep semantic information of text, and can address some problems that are difficult to be handled by traditional evaluation metrics (e.g. synonym substitution, utterance rearrangement) giving reasonable evaluation.

elements.id-string-486: This section presents the details of \textbf{FunMentor} for counter-intuitiveness understanding.
elements.id-string-487: FunMentor is an agent that refines a VLM's answer through multi-turn dialogues, ensuring it generates answers that best explain the given surprising content.
elements.id-string-488: The refining process comprises three components:
elements.id-string-490: Initially, FunMentor poses a series of inquiries to the VLM model it aims to assist, focusing on fact-aware questions to accurately comprehend the objective content of the video (e.g., FunMentor might ask: ``Please describe the items and characters appearing in each frame of the video'').
elements.id-string-491: This step is crucial because, without this preliminary context, FunMentor would have no knowledge of the video content and might be gullible to VLM's humorous explanations of the video.
elements.id-string-492: Thus, providing it with some factual clues is very important.
elements.id-string-494: FunMentor assesses VLMs' responses based on several key aspects: \textbf{1) Language Fluency}, ensuring responses are grammatically fluent; \textbf{2) Detail Accuracy}, verifying factual correctness in relation to the video's content; \textbf{3) Logical Reasoning}, checking for coherent logic and smooth transitions; and \textbf{4) Humorous Insight}, expecting responses to provide humor beyond a mere description of the video.
elements.id-string-495: If not passed, FunMentor will try to generate some feedback, which is explained below.
elements.id-string-497: Upon receiving unsatisfactory responses, FunMentor formulates constructive suggestions and tailored prompts, which are then sent back to the VLMs for revision, anticipating their improved answers.
elements.id-string-498: This process involves the agent analyzing the model's initial response, blending pre-defined prompts with the context of the original question, to generate specific feedback instructions.
elements.id-string-499: For example, FunMentor examines the issues in the VLM's response and advises on what should and shouldn't be included in the revised answer, guiding the VLM towards a more accurate and relevant reply.
elements.id-string-500: Fig. \ref{fig:funmentor} shows the pipeline of FunMentor.
